sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: **FaithWall** puts one verse from Psalm 91 on your iPhone lock screen: search Psalm 91, pick the verse, and the app applies it as your wallpaper through an Apple Shortcut. Each of the psalm's 16 verses fits on its own. The whole psalm doesn't read in a glance.

sections.text: For a **Psalm 91 wallpaper iPhone** setup, choose one verse, not the whole psalm. Start with 91:2, the line written for you to say yourself, or 91:11, the short promise about angels that most readers already know. FaithWall finds the verse and keeps it on your lock screen until you pick another. Below, all sixteen King James verses are checked for fit, with the reasons behind the picks and both ways to set one. For the wider system behind a verse on your lock screen, see the [daily Scripture lock screen guide](/daily-scripture-lock-screen).
The FaithWall setup for a Psalm 91 lock screen

Setting a Psalm 91 verse takes four steps in the app, and the verse stays on the lock screen until you choose a different one. The app lays the text out below the clock and applies it with an Apple Shortcut, so there is no image to crop or save to Photos first.

items: Find Psalm 91 with search or the built-in Bible browser (Psalms, chapter 91), in KJV or any of the 24 translations, and pick your verse. The app then runs an Apple Shortcut that applies it, and iOS shows Shortcuts for a moment.
For a different background or text style, tap Update Wallpaper Now in Settings. The verse stays until you pick another.

sections.content: **No app yet?** The free [Bible verse wallpaper maker](/bible-verse-wallpaper-maker) on this site builds one image in your browser. That image keeps its one verse until you make a new one.

Which Psalm 91 verses fit under the clock?

All sixteen fit, one verse at a time. The wallpaper maker on this site lays out text by a fixed rule, so the check can be repeated: on November 23, 2026, at the standard iPhone size (1179 × 2556 pixels) and the default Pure black style, every verse of Psalm 91 set at the full type size. Only the line count changed.

The maker keeps the top 35% of the screen clear for the clock, date and widgets and the bottom 12% for the flashlight and camera buttons, then sets the verse as large as the space between allows. Whatever makes your **Psalm 91 wallpaper iPhone** image, those two zones are where text gets covered. Counted in the site's own KJV text, the verses run from 12 to 25 words:

Line count follows letters more than words. Verse 1 has one word fewer than verse 2 but 14 more characters, so it takes a fifth line. On the Pro Max size (1290 × 2796), verses 1, 7, 11 and 12 each drop a line. Pairs still fit: 91:1-2 runs 39 words in eight lines, 91:11-12 runs 32 in seven. The whole psalm, 288 words, fits only at 45% of the full size, in 26 lines: readable in the editor, not in the second it takes to check the time.

sections.text: Which Psalm 91 verse should you set first?

Set Psalm 91:2 first, 91:11 second, and 91:4 when you need the picture of shelter. That is my order after reading all sixteen with a lock screen in mind: each one makes sense without the verses around it, each reads in one or two glances, and together they carry the psalm's three ideas of refuge, protection and covering.

You would not be alone in reaching for it. 18.5 million people a day turn to the Bible on YouVersion, per YouVersion's 2026 search report, and the single term they searched most this year was Psalm 91. All sixteen of its verses also sit in the top 25 of Bible Gateway's latest year-end list of most-read verses.

**Psalm 91:2 is the one to say back.** It is written in the first person, as something you say yourself: the Lord is my refuge and my fortress. Twenty words, four lines. Verse 1 is the famous opening, but it describes someone else, the one who dwells in the secret place. Verse 2 is the answer. If you want both, the pair still fits at full size.
I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust.

**Psalm 91:11 is the short one most people know.** It ranks highest of the psalm's verses on Bible Gateway's latest year-end list, at #8, and at 16 words it takes four lines, three on a Pro Max. Read it as trust, not a dare. In Matthew 4:6 the devil quoted 91:11-12 to tempt Jesus to throw himself from the pinnacle of the temple, and Jesus answered from Deuteronomy: "Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God."

**Psalm 91:4 is the picture.** Feathers and wings say shelter faster than any abstract word, and the verse ends with truth as a shield and buckler. At 22 words and five lines it asks for two glances, which is the price of the image.
He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.

Three I would leave for later. Verse 7, a thousand falling at thy side, is better read with the verses around it than alone on a screen you glance at. Verses 14 and 15 are God speaking, at 25 and 24 words and five lines each. Verse 16 is the shortest at 12 words, but its "him" points back to verses 14 and 15, so on its own it has no one to point to.

sections.title: One line, many glances
sections.content: Psalm 91 is a psalm to come back to, and the lock screen is the screen you come back to most. Set one verse there and you read it every time you check the time, without opening a Bible app.

sections.text: Why a saved Psalm 91 image falls short

Most Psalm 91 wallpapers online are made for a feed, not a lock screen. Many put verse 1 over a landscape photo or set the whole psalm in small type, and on the phone the clock lands on the first line, a widget covers the reference, or the crop cuts the last words. A **Psalm 91 wallpaper iPhone** image only works when the text sits in the space the clock leaves free.

**FaithWall takes the layout off your hands.** You pick the verse, the app sets it in the space below the clock and applies it, and it stays until you choose the next one. When the season changes, pick another line from the same psalm: 91:5 when nights feel long, 91:2 when you need to say it again.
For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.

Psalm 91 sits well beside Psalm 23. The [Psalm 23 wallpaper setup](/blog/psalm-23-wallpaper-iphone) works through which lines of the shepherd psalm fit a lock screen, and if fear is what brought you to Psalm 91, the [lock screen verses for anxiety](/blog/lock-screen-verses-for-anxiety) gather ten more short ones.
